name: Agomelatine
lead: Agomelatine is a prescription antidepressant developed by Servier and sold as Valdoxan and Thymanax. It acts as an agonist at melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors and a neutral antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2C receptors, which makes it the first melatonergic antidepressant.[2][3][9][13] It was authorised in the European Union in 2009 and later in Australia and other countries, but it is not approved by the US FDA.[13]

Its connection to appearance runs through sleep, mood and recovery: depression and disrupted sleep both show in the face and body (tired skin, puffy eyes, lost training consistency), and agomelatine is a drug that targets mood while shifting circadian markers such as sleep phase and melatonin onset in depressed patients.[13] No study has examined it for appearance outcomes, and it is a prescription medicine used for depression and, in Australia, generalised anxiety.[13]

Comparative research includes the 2018 Lancet network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants, which placed agomelatine among the better-tolerated agents, and a 2013 Cochrane review that found it about as effective as other antidepressants.[4][13] Liver enzyme monitoring is part of its prescribing because of reported transaminase rises.[13]

paras: Agomelatine is authorised in the EU for major depressive episodes in adults.[1][13] In Australia it is also approved for generalised anxiety disorder; elsewhere GAD use is off-label, and a 2023 review of anxiety treatment lists agomelatine among agents showing efficacy there.[13][16] It is not recommended in the EU or Australia for people under 18, although a 2022 Lancet Psychiatry trial in ages 7 to 17 reported benefit over placebo, and it is not recommended in dementia, pregnancy or breastfeeding.[13]

Smaller studies have examined agomelatine in circadian rhythm sleep disorders, ADHD with sleep problems, obsessive-compulsive disorder and sleep in obstructive sleep apnoea; these are off-label investigations.[13][17][18][19][20] A 2019 Cochrane review made no recommendation for or against it in seasonal affective disorder.[13]

The 2013 Cochrane review found agomelatine about as effective as other antidepressants with fewer discontinuations because of side effects, and a 2014 meta-analysis of published and unpublished trials reported a standardised mean difference of 0.24 versus standard antidepressants.[13] The 2018 network meta-analysis by Cipriani and colleagues found it comparable to most agents and one of two antidepressants with fewer all-cause discontinuations than placebo.[4][13] A 2007 pooled analysis reported larger drug-placebo differences in severe depression.[13]
Reanalyses have raised concerns about publication bias; Howland (2011) and Koesters (2013) concluded the benefit over placebo was small.[13]

Common effects (1 to 10 percent) include headache, nausea, dizziness, somnolence, diarrhoea, insomnia, fatigue, anxiety and raised liver enzymes, mostly mild and appearing in the first two weeks.[13] Reviews describe a low rate of sexual dysfunction compared with SSRIs and SNRIs, and an Australian review places agomelatine among the antidepressants with the least risk.[7][13][14] Weight change tends to be smaller than with SSRIs, and discontinuation does not require tapering.[13]

Liver safety is the main concern. After Servier's 2012 disclosure to the European Medicines Agency, labelling recommended liver tests before starting, periodically during treatment and after dose changes.[13] A 2016 pooled analysis of 7,605 patients found 36.1 percent of those with raised enzymes normalised without stopping, and a 2019 study found no difference in acute liver injury between agomelatine and citalopram users, a result the article notes may reflect precautionary monitoring.[13] Rare events include mania, suicidal ideation and liver failure. It is contraindicated in hepatic impairment and with strong CYP1A2 inhibitors such as fluvoxamine, and alcohol may increase hepatotoxicity risk.[13]

Agomelatine binds MT1 and MT2 receptors with very high affinity (Ki about 0.1 nM) and is a weak antagonist at 5-HT2C and 5-HT2B receptors.[13] A 2003 preclinical study showed the 5-HT2C blockade enhances frontocortical dopaminergic and noradrenergic activity, giving rise to the label norepinephrine-dopamine disinhibitor.[3][13] Some authors dispute the clinical importance of 5-HT2C antagonism at therapeutic doses, since no human receptor occupancy studies have been done.[13] In depressed patients, agomelatine increases slow-wave sleep and advances sleep phase, the fall in body temperature and melatonin onset.[13]

Absorption is at least 80 percent but bioavailability is about 1 percent because of first-pass metabolism, mainly by CYP1A2 (about 90 percent) and CYP2C9/2C19; half-life is 1 to 2 hours with no accumulation, and about 80 percent is excreted renally as metabolites.[13]
Agomelatine resembles melatonin but replaces the indole ring with a naphthalene bioisostere.[13]

Servier discovered and developed agomelatine; a 2010 Nature Reviews Drug Discovery article describes it as the first melatonergic antidepressant.[9][13] Servier submitted it to the EMA in March 2005 and the CHMP recommended refusal in July 2006 on efficacy grounds; a new application in September 2007 led to EU authorisation in February 2009, and Australia followed in August 2010.[13] Servier licensed US rights to Novartis in 2006, and US development stopped in October 2011 after the final trial results.[13]

Agomelatine is prescription-only in the EU, UK (POM), Australia (S4) and Brazil (Class C1), with low dependence liability.[13] No looksmaxxing community discussion of agomelatine was identified; its presence in this wiki reflects its sleep and circadian mechanism.

Phase 3 placebo-controlled trials in major depression include NCT00411242 (503 participants) and trials of a sublingual formulation, including a 52-week open-label safety study (NCT01156415, 837 participants, terminated).[10][11][15] The 2018 Lancet network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants compared agomelatine with other drugs for acute treatment of adult depression.[4] A 2025 multicentre randomised trial tested agomelatine as an add-on to SSRIs or SNRIs.[21]

Smaller registered trials examined depression with fibromyalgia, cardiovascular effects, depression in schizophrenia and post-stroke depression prevention.[5][6][12] A small placebo-controlled study in ten ADHD patients found agomelatine superior to placebo and less effective than methylphenidate, and a 2025 randomised trial combined electroacupuncture with agomelatine for post-stroke insomnia.[17][22] No studies were found on agomelatine for appearance outcomes.

card.summary: A melatonin-linked antidepressant sold in Europe, not the US; no appearance evidence.
card.note: Liver enzyme monitoring is part of prescribing; not FDA approved.

quick.overview:
Agomelatine is a prescription antidepressant authorised in the EU and some other countries but not in the US. It acts on melatonin receptors as well as a serotonin receptor.

No studies tie it to appearance, and it appears here because of its sleep and circadian angle.
quick.mechanism: It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors and blocks 5-HT2C receptors, which preclinical work links to increased dopamine and noradrenaline in the frontal cortex.
quick.risks: Reported effects include headache, nausea, dizziness and sleepiness. Raised liver enzymes have been reported, so liver testing is part of use, and it is contraindicated in hepatic impairment.

chain: Shifts sleep timing and mood in depressed patients
Better rest and mood that carry into skin, energy and training
angle.text: Agomelatine is a prescription antidepressant with a sleep-and-circadian mechanism. Where it is prescribed for depression, improved sleep and mood are the route by which it could affect how rested and well a person looks; it has not been tested for appearance directly.
